Name: Adam
Transcript: Good to see you again. Last time was March, before the season started. So, to begin, what's the plot like for you now, at midsummer?

Name: Arlo
Transcript: Better than I expected and worse than I hoped. Which I think is probably the most honest sentence I've said all year. Some days I come back calm. Properly calm, like something's been taken out of my head and put down somewhere. And other days I spend an hour at the plot worrying about slugs instead of worrying about work. So I haven't stopped worrying. I've just moved the worry. Relocated it. It's the same worry, it's just outdoors now, and it's about lettuces.

Name: Adam
Transcript: You've moved the worry. Tell me about that.

Name: Arlo
Transcript: So in May the slugs ate every lettuce I had. Every single one, in one night. Twenty-four lettuces. I'd grown them from seed on my windowsill, I'd hardened them off, I'd done it all by the book, literally by the book, and I went down on the Saturday and there were just stalks. Little white stalks and slime. And I took it personally. I really did. I took it as a personal attack. That night I went back at eleven o'clock with a head torch and a bucket, and I picked slugs off for two hours. Two hours. In the dark. Which is not, I'm aware, the behaviour of a calm person.

Name: Adam
Transcript: What was that like, out there in the dark?

Name: Arlo
Transcript: It was very strange. I was standing there with the head torch, picking slugs into a bucket, and I had this thought. I thought, this is my job. This is literally my job. Something's broken, it's urgent, and I'm on call. I'd brought the queue with me. I'd built a little night shift for myself, in a field. And I laughed. Out loud, in the dark, on my own, which if anyone had seen it would have been quite worrying. Despairing and funny at the same time. And then I went home at one in the morning, and I slept. Straight away. Which I never do after work. So, you know. Swings and roundabouts.

Name: Adam
Transcript: You said you'd brought the queue with you.

Name: Arlo
Transcript: Yeah. I think that's what I do. I take the queue everywhere. It's not really about work, it's a way of being. Everything is a problem waiting for me to fix it, and if I'm not fixing something I'm waiting for the next thing to break. At the plot I thought there'd be no queue. Soil and weather, I said, nobody can email me. But the slugs emailed me. The blackfly emailed me. The weather emails me every morning, I check the forecast like it's my inbox. I've basically set up an inbox in a field.

Name: Adam
Transcript: Tell me about a calm day.

Name: Arlo
Transcript: Last Tuesday. I went at six, before work. There was mist lying on the plots, really low, so the bean poles were sticking up out of it, and nobody about, not even Des. And I tied in the tomatoes. Just that. They'd got leggy and they needed tying to their canes, so I went down the row with string, one by one, tying them in. And I didn't think about anything at all, for an hour. Nothing. I couldn't tell you the last time that happened. Years. The smell of the tomato leaves, that green smell that gets on your fingers, and the string, and the mist. That's all there was.

Name: Adam
Transcript: Didn't think about anything at all. What was that like?

Name: Arlo
Transcript: It's hard to describe, because there was nothing to describe. That's the point of it. It was like somebody had closed all my tabs. All forty. I didn't do it, I didn't try to do it, it just happened, while I was busy with the string. And when I noticed, at the end of the row, I was a bit scared to move. In case they all came back. I stood there holding the last bit of string very still, like you would with a bird that's landed near you. And then I looked at my phone to check the time and they all came back. Every one. But for an hour, they were closed.

Name: Adam
Transcript: You were scared to move in case they came back.

Name: Arlo
Transcript: Yeah. Because I know I can't make it happen. I tried, the next day. Went at six, same time, tied in more tomatoes, same string. And nothing. My head was going the whole time, the queue, the emails, a thing someone said in a meeting. You can't schedule it. Which is very annoying for someone like me, because scheduling things is basically my whole personality. But it happened, once, so I know it's possible. That's new. I didn't know it was possible. I genuinely thought my head just did that all the time, for ever, and that was the deal.

Name: Adam
Transcript: You didn't know it was possible.

Name: Arlo
Transcript: No. I'd sort of accepted it. That my head was a server room. Always on, fans going, little lights blinking. I thought that was just the hardware I'd been given. And then for an hour, in the tomatoes, the fans stopped. And I thought, oh. So it can stop. It's not broken, it's just never been turned off. That's a different problem. I don't know how to solve it yet. But it's a different problem, and I quite like having a different problem.

Name: Adam
Transcript: And the people there?

Name: Arlo
Transcript: I keep to myself. I have my headphones in. I'll be honest, half the time there's nothing playing. They're just in. They're a sign. Do not disturb. Des waves, every time, and I wave back. Sometimes he says something and I take one out and say pardon and he says it again, and it's usually about the weather, and I put it back in. I know I should talk more. My therapist says it's half the point, the community thing. But I'm not there for people. I'm there to not be there for people.

Name: Adam
Transcript: Not there for people.

Name: Arlo
Transcript: Mostly. Although. There's a group of them on a Saturday morning, the regulars, they have a flask by the water butts and they stand around for about an hour not doing any gardening at all, just talking. And I watch them a bit. From my plot. With my headphones in. And I'm a bit, I don't know. Envious isn't quite it. It's like watching a party through a window. And I've chosen the window. I could go out there. I could just walk over. Nobody's stopping me. But I've chosen the window, and I keep choosing it.

Name: Adam
Transcript: You've chosen the window. What keeps you choosing it?

Name: Arlo
Transcript: If I go over, I have to be someone. Do you know what I mean? I'd have to be the new bloke, the young one, the one who works in computers. I'd have to have opinions about compost. And then they'd know me, and then they'd notice when I'm not there, and then I'd have to explain. At the window nobody notices anything. I'm just the bloke with headphones on fourteen. That's quite restful, actually. Being nobody in particular. I've spent a lot of my life having to be somebody on calls.

Name: Adam
Transcript: What do you make of Des?

Name: Arlo
Transcript: I don't know. I don't really know him. He's been there forty years, someone said. He's always there, whatever time I go, six in the morning, eight at night, he's there. Pottering. Sitting in his doorway with a radio. I sort of assumed he's just one of those old men who likes his allotment. I haven't asked. I don't ask people things, at the moment. If you ask people things they ask you things back.

Name: Adam
Transcript: What's gone well?

Name: Arlo
Transcript: The tomatoes, oddly. I've got more than I can eat. I have tomatoes for breakfast now, which is a sentence I never thought I'd say. And I took a bag into work on our office day, the one day a month we go in. Just put them on the kitchen counter with a note, help yourself. And people looked at me like I'd grown a second head. In a nice way, mostly. And one woman, Priya, from the sales side, she came and found me at my desk and asked how I got them so sweet. And we talked for twenty minutes. About tomatoes. About her dad's greenhouse. Twenty minutes. That's the longest conversation I've had at work in a year that wasn't about a ticket.

Name: Adam
Transcript: What was that like?

Name: Arlo
Transcript: Weird. Nice. Mostly nice. I didn't have to think about what to do with my face, because we were both just talking about tomatoes. The tomatoes did the talking, sort of. I had something to say that wasn't a problem. I didn't realise I didn't have that. Everything I say at work is a problem or a fix for a problem. And this was just, here are some tomatoes, they're nice, I grew them. I walked back to my desk feeling about two inches taller. Over tomatoes.

Name: Adam
Transcript: Something to say that wasn't a problem.

Name: Arlo
Transcript: Yeah. I've been thinking about that since. I think the plot's the first thing in years that I've got something to say about that isn't a complaint. If you ask me about work I'll tell you what's broken. If you ask me about the flat I'll tell you about the damp. If you ask me how I am, I've got a whole paragraph, and it's mostly therapy. But tomatoes. I can tell you about tomatoes and it's just, nice. It's good news. I didn't have any good news. Now I've got tomatoes.

Name: Adam
Transcript: In March you said you didn't want the plot to be another thing you fail at, with an audience. How is that now?

Name: Arlo
Transcript: Still there. Still feels watched. Des told me in June my runner beans needed proper sticks, not the bamboo I'd used, and I went straight to, he thinks I'm useless, he's been watching me get it wrong for months. And then the next day there were six hazel poles leaning on my shed. From him. No note. Just poles. So I've decided Des is not a performance review. I'm working on it. And the slugs, weirdly, helped with the audience thing. Because everyone had slugs. Everyone lost their lettuces. It wasn't me being uniquely bad, it was just May. Which is a strange thing to be comforted by. Collective slug failure.

Name: Adam
Transcript: Does the plot come up with your therapist?

Name: Arlo
Transcript: Every week. I report back. And she's pleased, she's really pleased, and it's slightly annoying how pleased she is. Because it makes it feel like homework again. Like I'm handing in my plot to be marked. And I do catch myself going because I said I would. Because I'll have to tell her on Thursday if I didn't. Not because I want to go. Some weeks I'm going for her, not for me. I don't know what to do with that, really.

Name: Adam
Transcript: Going for her, not for you. What's that like?

Name: Arlo
Transcript: A bit hollow. Those are the bad days, usually. I go, and I do the jobs, and I'm thinking about what I'll say on Thursday. I'm narrating it to her in my head while I'm doing it. Went to the plot, did the watering, felt quite calm. And I'm not calm, I'm writing a report. So then I'm doing the plot and the report about the plot at the same time, and that's two jobs. The good days are the ones where I forget to tell her. Where I get to Thursday and she asks and I realise I didn't think about her once.

Name: Adam
Transcript: And your body, how has that been?

Name: Arlo
Transcript: My hands are completely different. Calluses, here, look. Proper ones. And I've got a farmer's tan on one arm, my left arm, because that's the one that's out when I'm tying things, and the other arm's still basically IT. Pale, office arm. I look like two different people stitched together. And I sleep on plot days. Not every day, but on plot days, I sleep. My body seems to know the difference between tired from the plot and tired from the screen. The screen tired is sort of buzzy. The plot tired is heavy and it lets you go.

Name: Adam
Transcript: Is there anything else, about the plot now, that I haven't asked?

Name: Arlo
Transcript: Only that I'm still going. That was my one target, in March. Still going in October. And it's July, and I'm still going. So I'm on track. I'm aware I've just described my own life as being on track against a target. I can hear it. But yeah. Still going.
